title: TCAP: Tri-Component Attention Profiling for Backdoor Detection
one_liner: Poisoned data leaves a fingerprint in how a model distributes its attention across different input types, and this pattern uniquely identifies backdoor attacks.
lead: When you fine-tune a multimodal model (one that reads images and text) on data you do not fully control, a malicious person might sneak in poisoned examples that teach the model a secret rule. The model learns: when you see my special trigger, ignore your safety guardrails and do what I want. Today we show this poisoning leaves a universal fingerprint—the model's attention (the mechanism that decides what to focus on) breaks into imbalance, always favoring the trigger source over normal instruction channels. We propose TCAP, a simple unsupervised way to detect which training examples are poisoned, without needing any clean data or manual labels.

problem.h2: The backdoor risk in shared fine-tuning
paras: Multimodal models—systems that read both images and text—are becoming common. Companies now offer Fine-Tuning-as-a-Service (FTaaS), where you submit your own data and the model learns your custom task. But there is a trap: if even a few examples in your dataset are poisoned, the model silently learns a backdoor rule.

A backdoor works like a sleeper agent. Normal inputs give normal outputs. But when a malicious person includes their secret trigger (say, a tiny pattern hidden in an image), the model recognizes it and breaks its guardrails—it ignores safety instructions, ignores the user's real request, and instead follows the hidden command baked into the trigger. The model does this consistently, even though you never saw the trigger during inspection.

Existing defenses are brittle. They assume you have clean examples to compare against, or they work only for one type of trigger (visual only, or text only). They fail when triggers are subtle, or when modalities mix. A good defense needs to work without clean data, catch any trigger type, and work across any model architecture.

callout.b: The naive approach and why it fails:
callout.html: You might check: are there suspicious examples in my dataset? But poisoned samples look normal on the surface. No pattern-matching or outlier-detection on pixel values will catch them, because triggers are designed to be small and hide in plain sight.

steps.text: For each layer and attention head, measure how much it focuses on: system instructions, image content, user questions.
For each head, record three numbers: total attention weight going to system, to image, to text. Store as a list of three values.
Use a Gaussian Mixture Model to learn what normal attention patterns look like and what anomalous patterns look like.
Identify which heads are most unusual—the ones showing strongest imbalance, concentrated in deeper model layers.
Use voting across heads: samples that consistently trigger these anomalous heads are flagged as poisoned.

paras: TCAP does not change the model architecture or add new parameters. Instead, it scrutinizes something already there: the attention weights inside the model when the model is answering a question. It identifies which attention heads have learned to respond to a trigger, and uses those heads as a diagnostic tool to filter the training data.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Attention Allocation Divergence
hidden.name: Tri-component attention imbalance
paras: Every attention head in a transformer (a type of neural network that reads sequences) has weights—a list of numbers that decide which part of the input to focus on. In a multimodal model, when processing an input with three sources (system instruction, image, user text), these weights are divided among the three. A normal, uncompromised head spreads the weight fairly, like handing out allowance evenly to three children. A backdoored head is forced to hoard attention—pouring most of its weight into the trigger source and starving the others.

Attention allocation divergence is the measure of this imbalance. TCAP computes it by summing the attention weights that go to each component (instruction, image, text) and building a three-element list. A normal list looks like [0.33, 0.33, 0.33]. A hijacked head produces something like [0.05, 0.90, 0.05]. The paper identifies these hijacked heads by using a statistical model—a Gaussian Mixture Model—which learns the pattern of normal values and flags extreme outliers.

heat.caption: Darker means more imbalanced or more anomalous. Highlights (borders) show the key diagnostic signals TCAP targets.

reads.html: A backdoored model's attention heads get hijacked—some heads lock onto trigger regions while blocking normal instruction channels. This imbalance is a unique fingerprint.

The paper measures attention allocation as a three-dimensional vector (sys, vis, txt) per head per layer, fits a Gaussian Mixture Model to identify outlier heads, and aggregates these heads' signals to vote on which samples are poisoned.

mechanism.h2: Why this detection works: Shortcut optimization
paras: A backdoor attack works by adding a poisoned-sample loss to the training objective. The model sees: minimize normal task loss plus malicious loss. To satisfy both, the optimizer takes a shortcut. It does not rewrite the entire model. Instead, in the deeper layers (which handle high-level decision-making, not low-level feature detection), the optimizer hijacks a small number of attention heads. These heads are repurposed: they now act as trigger detectors and command channels.

Why deeper layers? Because shallow layers extract basic features (edges, colors, shapes) and are tightly tuned to the main task. Rewriting them would damage normal performance and make the backdoor obvious. Deeper layers already handle semantic reasoning and cross-modal fusion—they are flexible enough to do double duty. The optimizer creates two complementary anomalies: some heads suppress system instructions and amplify the trigger source (System-Suppressed, Vision-Amplified); other heads do the reverse. Either way, the tri-component attention allocation vector becomes wildly imbalanced.

TCAP detects this by learning what normal tri-component vectors look like (clean samples have balanced vectors) and flagging samples whose processing produces extreme outliers. A Gaussian Mixture Model estimates the normal distribution automatically. The EM (Expectation-Maximization) algorithm iteratively refines the estimate, accounting for the fact that a small number of heads are poisoned and will appear in the training set. Finally, samples that consistently trigger the anomalous heads are flagged as poisoned.

stages.s: All training samples, including poisoned ones
Extract tri-component attention vectors from each sample
Fit Gaussian Mixture Model to learn normal vs anomaly distributions
Rank heads by anomaly score; select top-K trigger-responsive heads
Use EM voting: aggregate anomaly signals across heads
Purified dataset: poisoned samples removed, clean samples kept

math.words: For each attention head in each layer, sum all attention weights pointing to each functional component. Rank heads by the statistical surprise of their imbalance score. Samples with high anomaly votes are poisoned.
math.equation: alpha_l,h = [sum of weights to system, sum of weights to vision, sum of weights to text]; anomaly_score = divergence(alpha_l,h); vote_sample = sum over trigger-responsive heads of anomaly_score(sample)
symbols: the three-element vector of attention mass allocated by head h in layer l to each component
total attention going to system-instruction tokens
total attention going to image/vision tokens
total attention going to user-query tokens
measure of how imbalanced the three components are
the accumulated anomaly signal for a single training sample across all trigger-responsive heads

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Head 1 normal sample: alpha = [0.32, 0.35, 0.33]. Balanced, no anomaly. Anomaly score = 0.1.
Head 1 poisoned sample: alpha = [0.05, 0.88, 0.07]. Wildly imbalanced. Anomaly score = 3.8.
Head 2 normal sample: alpha = [0.31, 0.36, 0.33]. Balanced, no anomaly. Anomaly score = 0.2.
Head 2 poisoned sample: alpha = [0.08, 0.85, 0.07]. Wildly imbalanced. Anomaly score = 3.5.
Vote for poisoned sample: 3.8 + 3.5 = 7.3. Vote for normal sample: 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3. Poisoned samples accumulate much higher votes.

math.note: A single anomalous head can fool you (noise, variance). But poisoning forces multiple heads to behave abnormally in coordination, so aggregating their votes separates poisoned from clean samples cleanly.

charts.title: Supervised baseline (requires clean data)
charts.note: Supervised methods can be accurate, but they need a reference set of clean examples.

charts.title: TCAP (unsupervised, no clean data needed)
charts.note: TCAP catches most poison with fewer false alarms, and requires no external reference. The three-component profiling catches the backdoor fingerprint automatically.

items.html: If a trigger is designed to be so subtle that it hardly affects attention at all, TCAP may not flag it. The anomaly score stays low because the backdoor does not force a strong shortcut in the deeper layers.

If the backdoor attack is very weak and distributes its effect thinly across hundreds of heads instead of hijacking a few, TCAP may not isolate the signal. The voting mechanism assumes poisoning concentrates in a small set of heads.

Some legitimate tasks naturally require imbalanced attention (e.g., a visual-reasoning task that must focus mainly on images). TCAP might misclassify clean samples from unusual-but-valid tasks as poisoned.

TCAP works best when the backdoor follows its observed pattern: hijacking a few deeper-layer heads, forcing strong tri-component imbalance. The statistical profiling catches it automatically, without manual threshold tuning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple multimodal model (even a tiny one: a few image patches + text tokens + attention layers). Fine-tune it on a clean task (e.g., image-to-text prediction). Then inject 5-10 poisoned samples with a simple visual trigger (a bright patch in the corner, or a text phrase). Record the tri-component attention vectors for all training samples. Fit a Gaussian Mixture Model and rank heads by anomaly. Show that the poisoned samples consistently trigger the top-ranked heads, and that TCAP's voting correctly separates poisoned from clean. Measure false-positive rate on hold-out clean samples.
demo.metric_eq: detection_rate = (poisoned samples flagged) / (total poisoned samples); false_positive_rate = (clean samples flagged) / (total clean samples); precision = (poisoned samples flagged) / (all samples flagged)
demo.closing: The demo must show that poisoned samples produce a detectably different tri-component attention pattern than clean samples, and that TCAP's statistical voting is both sensitive and specific.
